The text investigates the geometry of surfaces generated by the motion of closed strings in a spacetime manifold. A closed string sweeps out a two-dimensional surface, often called a worldsheet, as it evolves through spacetime. The main objective is to study how such surfaces vary and how nearby string worldsheets deviate from one another under small perturbations.

The analysis is based on the Nambu-Goto string action, which is the natural generalization of the point-particle action to extended one-dimensional objects. This action is proportional to the area of the worldsheet swept out by the string. By requiring the Nambu-Goto action to be stationary under variations of the embedding of the string worldsheet into the spacetime manifold, one obtains the equations governing the dynamics of the string.

From this variational principle, the geodesic surface equation is derived. This equation plays a role analogous to the geodesic equation for point particles. While a point particle traces out a one-dimensional geodesic curve, a string traces out a two-dimensional surface whose area is extremal. The resulting geodesic surface equation therefore describes the condition that the worldsheet be an extremal surface in the surrounding spacetime.

The text then studies variations of these geodesic surfaces. By considering a one-parameter family of nearby worldsheets and examining the infinitesimal separation between them, the geodesic surface deviation equation is obtained. This equation generalizes the usual geodesic deviation equation from curves to string worldsheets. It describes how neighboring extremal surfaces accelerate away from or toward one another due to the curvature of the ambient spacetime. The deviation vector field satisfying this equation is shown to be a Jacobi field, meaning that it represents an infinitesimal variation through geodesic surfaces.

Finally, an index form for geodesic surfaces is introduced. This index form provides a bilinear expression associated with variations of the worldsheet and is used to analyze the stability and focusing properties of geodesic surfaces. In particular, it allows one to discuss the existence of conjugate strings along the surface. Conjugate strings are the string-theoretic analogue of conjugate points in Riemannian geometry: they indicate where nontrivial Jacobi fields vanish at two distinct strings on the worldsheet, signaling a loss of local minimality or uniqueness of the extremal surface between them. Thus, the index form becomes a key tool for understanding the global and variational properties of string worldsheets in curved spacetime.

The study of strings moving through spacetime naturally leads to the geometry of surfaces rather than the geometry of curves. While the motion of a point particle is represented by a worldline, the motion of a closed string is represented by a two-dimensional worldsheet swept out in spacetime. A central problem in relativistic string dynamics is therefore to understand how such worldsheets are determined, how they vary under small deformations, and how their stability properties can be characterized geometrically.

This text examines these questions using the Nambu-Goto action, which measures the area of the worldsheet swept out by the string. By applying a variational principle to this action, one obtains the equations governing extremal surfaces in spacetime. These extremal surfaces are the string-theoretic analogues of geodesics in point-particle mechanics: just as a free particle follows a geodesic curve, a free relativistic string sweeps out a geodesic surface, or minimal surface, determined by the vanishing of its mean curvature.

The analysis then considers variations of such geodesic surfaces. In ordinary Riemannian or Lorentzian geometry, nearby geodesics are studied through the geodesic deviation equation, whose solutions are Jacobi fields. These fields describe how infinitesimally close geodesics separate or converge and play a crucial role in understanding conjugate points and stability. The text extends this framework to the case of closed strings by deriving corresponding deviation equations for families of worldsheets. The resulting Jacobi fields describe infinitesimal deformations of a geodesic surface through nearby string worldsheets.

A key part of the construction is the development of an index form for these string worldsheets. In point-particle geometry, the index form is a bilinear expression associated with the second variation of the length or energy functional, and it is used to analyze whether a geodesic locally minimizes distance. In the string setting, the analogous index form arises from the second variation of the Nambu-Goto action. It provides a tool for studying the stability of geodesic surfaces under perturbations and for detecting directions in which the area of the worldsheet can decrease.

The main result of the text is a geometric framework for defining and analyzing conjugate strings on geodesic surfaces. In the classical theory of geodesics, conjugate points occur when nontrivial Jacobi fields vanish at two points, signaling a failure of local minimality and the presence of focusing phenomena. For strings, the corresponding notion involves entire closed string configurations rather than individual points. A conjugate string is identified through the existence of nontrivial Jacobi fields satisfying appropriate boundary conditions along the worldsheet. Such fields indicate that neighboring geodesic surfaces intersect or focus in a string-like manner.

By extending concepts such as geodesic deviation, Jacobi fields, conjugate points, and the index form from point-particle theory to string dynamics, the text provides a systematic way to study the geometry and stability of relativistic string worldsheets. This framework clarifies how closed strings evolve as extremal surfaces in spacetime and how their variations encode information about focusing, instability, and the global structure of the space of string configurations. In this way, the work generalizes familiar tools from differential geometry and gravitational theory to the richer setting of extended objects.

**Using the Nambu-Goto Action**

Using the Nambu-Goto action is a fundamental approach in string theory for describing how a relativistic string moves through spacetime. Unlike a point particle, which traces out a one-dimensional path called a worldline, a string sweeps out a two-dimensional surface known as a worldsheet. The Nambu-Goto action measures the area of this worldsheet, making it a natural generalization of the action for a relativistic particle.

The action is named after Yoichiro Nambu and Tetsuo Goto, who helped develop early formulations of string dynamics. In simple terms, the Nambu-Goto action states that a string moves in such a way that the area of its worldsheet is minimized, similar to how a soap film forms a surface of minimal area.

Mathematically, the Nambu-Goto action is often written as:

\[
S = -T \int d^2\sigma \sqrt{-\det h_{ab}}
\]

Here, \(T\) is the string tension, \(\sigma\) represents the coordinates on the worldsheet, and \(h_{ab}\) is the induced metric on the worldsheet. The determinant of this metric gives information about the geometry of the surface traced by the string.

Using the Nambu-Goto action provides an elegant and geometrical way to describe strings. However, it can be difficult to work with because of the square root and determinant in the formula. For this reason, physicists often use an equivalent formulation called the Polyakov action, which is easier to handle mathematically while describing the same physics.

Overall, the Nambu-Goto action remains an important concept because it captures the basic idea that strings evolve by minimizing the area of the surfaces they sweep through spacetime.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief abstract for a paper on geodesic surface deviation for closed strings using the Nambu-Goto action.
counterfactuals.output: We present a study of geodesic surface deviation for closed strings governed by the Nambu–Goto action. By treating the string worldsheet as a two-dimensional extremal surface embedded in a curved background spacetime, we derive the linearized deviation equations describing how nearby closed-string worldsheets separate under infinitesimal perturbations. These equations generalize the geodesic deviation equation for point particles to extended one-dimensional objects, incorporating both intrinsic worldsheet geometry and the extrinsic curvature of the embedding. We analyze the role of background curvature in driving relative string deformation and discuss implications for the stability of classical closed-string configurations. The resulting framework provides a geometric tool for investigating perturbations of Nambu–Goto strings in curved spacetimes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize in one paragraph how the Nambu-Goto string action leads to geodesic surface equations, Jacobi fields, and conjugate strings.
counterfactuals.output: The Nambu–Goto action is proportional to the area of the string worldsheet swept out in spacetime, so varying the embedding of the string and requiring the first variation to vanish gives the equations of motion: the worldsheet must be an extremal surface, equivalently a “geodesic surface” whose mean extrinsic curvature vanishes, generalizing the geodesic equation for a point particle. Small deformations of such a classical worldsheet are described by the second variation of the Nambu–Goto action; the resulting linearized equations are the Jacobi equations, whose solutions are Jacobi fields representing infinitesimal separations between neighboring extremal worldsheets. If a nontrivial Jacobi field vanishes on two string configurations or boundary slices, those configurations are said to be conjugate strings, analogous to conjugate points along a geodesic; their presence signals a degeneracy of the second variation and marks where the extremal worldsheet may cease to be locally area-minimizing or dynamically stable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2
